rows: A harvestman has a single pair of eyes, set back to back on a small turret in the middle of its body. Each eye looks out to one side.
A harvestman's eyes probably give only a rough picture of light and dark. A large dark object makes a species of Leiobunum flee, and in the laboratory harvestmen move away from light.
The most photographed harvestman, Phalangium opilio, also carries two more pairs of eyes inside its body, both shrunk to traces. They may help set its daily clock.
In two cave harvestmen from New Zealand the eyes respond to ultraviolet, blue and green light, over a range of brightness of at least a hundred thousand to one.
Harvestmen find food, mates and enemies mostly by touching and tasting them with their first pair of legs and their palps, and they sense little from a distance.

No one has measured how much detail a harvestman sees. This view assumes coarse sight of a few large shapes, grey, clearest out to each side. The dim seam's width, and the buzz at a knock (&draw=buzz), are the app's.
The touch and taste of a harvestman's legs and palps carry most of what it knows, and the camera records neither.
